name: Elena Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for agreeing to this, Elena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and we don't campaign for anything. It's all confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. Could you start with a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a continuous miner in an underground potash mine, about a kilometre down. It's a machine with a big rotating drum of cutting picks that chews through the potash seam and loads it onto a conveyor, no blasting. I lead a crew of five, and for the last year I've also been on the pilot team testing a semi-automated miner that follows the seam by itself while I watch and correct it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the pilot work, honestly, it's like teaching a very strong, very stupid apprentice. I use AI tools every day, for the shift log, for checking the vibration data on the cutting drum, and to ask questions about the control software that the manual doesn't answer. What wears me out is the commute down, forty minutes in the cage and the ride to the face, and the noise.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Tomas is a pharmacist in town, and we've got Lukas, who's twelve, and Ida, who's nine. We have a mortgage, about ten years left, and decent savings, more than six months, plus a small share portfolio. On weekends I've started doing drone inspections of farm sheds and grain bins with a mate from the mine, just for fun and a bit of cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but not world-changing, which is about what I'd have guessed in a sober moment. At work I'd keep pushing the pilot because even small automation makes the job safer. Online I'd say people got carried away in both directions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it changes nothing for me, and that's fine. I'd be a bit disappointed not to see where the pilot could go. I'd still be the person on site who understands both the machine and the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the pilot and my normal crew work, and keep putting money into shares and the mortgage. The drone thing might grow a bit, maybe a few more farm clients. Nothing radical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the drone inspections. How did they start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mate Joe from the electrical crew bought a drone to film his kid's football. We realised farmers pay a fortune to get someone up on a roof to check grain bins, so we started doing it for a fraction of the price. Last month we did six farms and made about two thousand between us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, would that side business matter much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much, it'd stay a hobby with some pocket money. But I like having something that's mine, that I built. And honestly I learned more about software from that drone than from any course.

S0.say: Elena would say AI turned out useful but not world-changing, and that people got carried away in both directions. At work she'd keep pushing the automation pilot because even small automation makes the job safer.
S0.think: Privately it changes nothing for her, though she'd be a little disappointed not to see where the pilot could go. She'd remain the person on site who understands both the machine and the software.
S0.do: Keeps running the pilot and her crew, and keeps investing in shares and the mortgage. Lets the weekend drone inspection business grow slowly with a few more farm clients.
S0.quote: I learned more about software from that drone than from any course.
S0.fieldNote: Elena is an early adopter with a practical edge, already testing a semi-automated miner and running a small drone side business. The plateau leaves her calm and a bit bored. She likes building things that are hers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the realistic version, and the people who learn the new tools will be fine. At work I'd tell my crew to get on the pilot program while there's room. I'd say the company should pay for training, because that's cheaper than hiring from scratch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me. I'm already the one who knows the semi-automated miner best, so in steady change I'd likely become the person who supervises several of them, maybe from the surface. The bit I'd worry about is my crew, especially the older guys who don't want to learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a formal role on the automation team in the first year, with a pay bump. I'd do a short course in industrial control systems, probably online, about six months part-time. And I'd grow the drone business, maybe buy a second drone with a thermal camera for about eight thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. It feels like my moment, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry about older guys on the crew. Who exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kurt, mostly. He's fifty-seven, best operator I've ever seen on a miner, and he thinks the pilot is a gimmick. I'd try to get him to at least sit with me on a shift, because his feel for the seam is exactly what the software lacks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave mining for the drone business, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not with steady change. The mine would need people like me more, not less. The drones stay a side thing, maybe a bigger side thing.

S1.say: Elena would call steady change the realistic version and say people who learn the new tools will be fine. She'd urge her crew to join the pilot and argue the company should pay for training.
S1.think: Privately she sees it as good for her, likely supervising several semi-automated miners from the surface. Her worry is for older crew members who don't want to learn the new system.
S1.do: Asks for a formal role on the automation team with a pay rise in the first year and takes a six-month online course in industrial control systems. Spends about eight thousand on a thermal drone to grow the side business.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, as if this were her moment.
S1.quote: His feel for the seam is exactly what the software lacks.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change looks like a promotion for Elena, and she says so plainly. She values Kurt's feel for the seam as something the software lacks, which is a thoughtful view for an early adopter. The drone business stays a side project here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge shock and we need governments to move fast on income support and retraining. I'd tell people at work not to freeze, to start learning anything they can now. Online I'd try to keep people calm, but honestly it'd be hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me for the first time. If AI and robots can do almost anything, then supervising automated miners stops being a job too. My advantage, knowing the machines, buys me maybe a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd try to get onto the company's AGI rollout team, because someone has to install and check these systems at the start. I'd shift some shares into cash and pay down the mortgage hard. And I'd push the drone business, because even if robots can inspect a grain bin, a farmer might still want someone they know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Busy and anxious, the kind where you can't stop making lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the drone business might survive because farmers want someone they know. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half. Honestly, if a robot drone can do it cheaper, most farmers will take it. But some won't, and with two years I'd rather have a small business with loyal clients than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomas the first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we're better off than most, with his pharmacy job and our savings. Then I'd ask him if pharmacists are safe, and he'd probably say no. We'd sit at the kitchen table and work out how long we could last if both of us lost our jobs, probably three or four years.

S2.say: Elena would call it a huge shock and urge governments to move fast on income support and retraining. She'd tell colleagues not to freeze and to start learning anything they can.
S2.think: Privately it worries her for the first time, because supervising automated miners would stop being a job too. Her edge in understanding the machines would buy her only a year or two.
S2.do: Moves fast to join the company's AGI rollout team and shifts some shares into cash while paying the mortgage down hard. Pushes the drone business harder in the hope of keeping loyal farm clients.
S2.feel: Anxious and busy, unable to stop making lists.
S2.quote: My advantage, knowing the machines, buys me maybe a year or two.
S2.fieldNote: Even for an early adopter like Elena, two years is the first picture that bites. She stays active, moving money and chasing the rollout team. Her honest doubt about the drone business shows she isn't fooling herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make real changes if people start now. I'd want the government to fund retraining and the companies to share their plans. At work I'd say get on the automation side while you can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a good run for me. I'd get maybe three or four years supervising and installing these systems before they run themselves. That pays off the mortgage and builds up savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get onto the automation team in year one and do the control systems course straight away. I'd try to grow the drone business into a proper company with Joe, maybe with a couple of automated drones of our own by year three. And I'd keep investing, partly in the companies building the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd feel like I had a plan, but the end point still nags at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd invest in the robot companies. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Practical, honestly. If they're going to make the money, I'd rather some of it came to my family. I don't see it as betting against my mates, I see it as being realistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lukas, who'd be seventeen by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn to build and fix the machines, and also learn to deal with people. The ones who can do both will be fine. He loves robotics club, so he's halfway there already.

S3.say: Elena would say five years is enough for real change if people start now. She'd want government-funded retraining and companies sharing their plans, and tell colleagues to move onto the automation side.
S3.think: Privately she sees five years as a good run, with three or four years supervising and installing systems before they run themselves. That would pay off the mortgage and build savings.
S3.do: Joins the automation team in year one and starts the control systems course immediately. Grows the drone business into a proper company with Joe and keeps investing, partly in robot companies.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with a plan in place but the end point still nagging at her.
S3.quote: I don't see it as betting against my mates, I see it as being realistic.
S3.fieldNote: Elena treats investing in robot companies as plain realism, with none of the guilt some others carry. Five years suits her fast-moving style. Her advice to her son blends technical and people skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time if we plan, and there's no reason anyone should be blindsided. I'd want a sensible public plan for retraining and income support. I'd keep saying get on the automation side early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is a good deal for me. I'd have a long run in automation, the mortgage gone by year eight, the kids grown. I could see myself running the drone company full-time with robots doing the flying and me dealing with clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into automation in the first couple of years, then shift towards the drone company by about year six. I'd keep investing steadily, maybe more in property as well as shares. And I'd talk to Tomas about whether he wants to change direction too, maybe into something like health coaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, mostly. The worry is for others more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the others you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kurt, and guys like him who'll never touch a screen. And the young guys who think they'll be miners for forty years. Ten years is enough for them to change, but only if someone tells them straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell them straight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I already do. I tell the young ones on my crew to learn the software side, and some of them think I'm a bit much. I'd rather be annoying now than watch them get caught out.

S4.say: Elena would say a decade is plenty of time if people plan and nobody should be blindsided. She'd want a sensible public plan for retraining and income support and keep urging people onto the automation side early.
S4.think: Privately she sees ten years as a good deal, with a long run in automation and the mortgage gone by year eight. She pictures running the drone company full-time with robots flying and her handling clients.
S4.do: Moves into automation in the first couple of years and shifts towards the drone company by about year six. Invests steadily in shares and property and talks with Tomas about whether he should change direction too.
S4.feel: Calm and mostly hopeful, with worry aimed at others rather than herself.
S4.quote: I'd rather be annoying now than watch them get caught out.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Elena picture a full transition from miner to business owner. She's direct with young crew members about the need to learn software. Her calm here comes from her adaptability and her savings working together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because even my head start runs out. What would help is fast retraining money and some kind of income bridge, so people like me can move into new things without risking the house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about people like Kurt, who know things the machines don't. If we automate without learning from them first, we lose that forever. I'd want companies to pay the old hands to teach the software before they go.

headlineQuote: I'd want companies to pay the old hands to teach the software before they go.
portrait: Elena Bauer is a 43-year-old crew leader running a continuous miner a kilometre underground at a potash mine, and a member of the pilot team testing a semi-automated machine. She uses AI every day, runs a weekend drone inspection business with a colleague, and has a pharmacist husband, two kids, a mortgage and a share portfolio. In the milder pictures automation looks like her moment, and she'd move onto the automation team quickly. The two-year AGI picture makes her anxious because even her head start runs out, while ten years lets her picture becoming a full-time business owner. She respects veterans like Kurt and wants their knowledge captured before it's lost.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because even her head start in automation would run out within a year or two.
whatWouldHelp: Fast retraining money and an income bridge so people can move into new work without risking their homes.
